p.x:
Last summer, my family stayed at a hotel in Phuket for five nights. My mother chose it from a holiday brochure. My father wanted to stay at a campsite and sleep in a tent, but my mother said no! We had a double room for my parents and a small room for my sister and me. Our room was on the eighth floor, so we used the lift every day. From the balcony, we had a wonderful view of the sea.
The hotel had a big swimming pool, and there were free towels next to it. Every morning, my sister and I swam before breakfast. The staff at reception were very friendly. They gave us a map and told us about a local guide who could take tourists to the islands.
On the last day, we had to check out at 11 a.m. Our flight was in the evening, so we left our suitcases at the hotel and went to the beach. "Next year, let's stay longer!" said my sister.

Dear Manager,
I am writing to complain about my recent stay at the Sunshine Resort, which I booked as part of a package holiday. I chose your resort because the website described it as "peaceful, with excellent service". Unfortunately, my experience was very different.
When we arrived, the receptionist told us that our sea-view room was not ready, and that there were no other vacancies because it was peak season. We waited for three hours. Then we were given a room next to the kitchen, which was extremely noisy. I asked for an upgrade, but this was refused.
In addition, the excursion to the waterfall, which was advertised as a highlight of the tour, was cancelled without explanation. Instead, we were taken to a shopping centre that was not a tourist attraction at all. Frankly, a cheap hostel would have offered better value.
I would like a partial refund for the room and the excursion. I look forward to your reply.
Yours faithfully,
Daniel Brooks

Tourism is one of Thailand's most important industries, employing millions of people in hospitality, transport and retail. Visitors are drawn by exotic food, warm weather and the famous friendliness of local people. Yet the industry's success has created serious problems.
Popular destinations can become overwhelmed. Some picturesque islands have had to close temporarily to allow beaches and coral reefs to recover from overcrowding. In peak months, hotels are frequently overbooked, and prices rise sharply. Some once-charming streets have become tourist traps, full of overpriced souvenir shops selling goods made in other countries.
In response, there is growing interest in ecotourism and community-based travel. Instead of staying in an all-inclusive resort where every need is handled by a concierge, travellers stay with local families in secluded villages, eat home-cooked meals and learn traditional crafts. Supporters say this provides a more authentic experience and spreads income more fairly.
Another solution is encouraging people to travel off-peak. Visiting during the rainy season, for example, can mean lower prices, fewer crowds and greener landscapes. The challenge is to keep tourism profitable without destroying the very places that attract visitors in the first place.
